title: KV writer lease and async reclamation for paged/blocked KV cache
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Problem: Long-context workloads and heavy multi-tenant traffic are exposing two related failure modes in the current paged/blocked KV cache: 1) concurrent writers and eviction races cause inconsistent page state and rare corruptions under stress; 2) synchronous reclamation/compaction during eviction incurs stalls that interact badly with continuous batching and cause tail-latency spikes.

Proposal summary: Introduce a lightweight writer-lease protocol for KV page writers plus an asynchronous reclamation pipeline that reclaims and compacts freed page fragments off the hot inference path. The writer-lease prevents concurrent conflicting updates to the same page block, and the async reclamation moves expensive operations (compaction, cross-shard coalescing) to background workers that throttle against GPU memory pressure signals.

Key goals: reduce eviction-related stalls, eliminate writer-induced state races, lower OOM/eviction events under bursty traffic, and preserve low single-request latency for streaming/continuous batches.

Core ideas (high level):
- Writer lease: each KV block has a small lease token (32-bit sequence + owner id). Writers acquire the lease before in-place updates (KV insert / growth). Lease acquisition is optimistic and falls back to copy-on-write when contended. Leases are time-bounded (ms) and renewed by the owning worker while active.
- Epoch-based async reclamation: freed slots are queued into per-GPU reclamation rings with epoch tags. Background reclaim workers perform compaction/coalescing and GPU-side memcpy in bounded chunks, relying on epoch guarantees so in-flight readers are never invalidated.
- Prefetch profiles + active-pin: continuous batching informs prefetcher which page ranges are hot for the next N micro-batches; hot pages are pinned (resident) during batch execution to avoid mid-batch eviction. Prefetch policy has profiles (short, medium, long) tuned from telemetry.
- Back-pressure integration: the reclamation workers subscribe to memory-pressure metrics (resident_set_ratio, fragmentation_score). When pressure is high, reclamation increases aggressiveness and signals scheduler to reduce batch size or reduce prefetch depth.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Lease cost vs contention safety: adding leases adds metadata and a small fast-path check, which increases write latency by ~0.3-0.6ms in microbenchmarks, but eliminates rare corruption risk and reduces heavy tail events during high concurrency. We prefer predictable micro-latency over occasional faster uncontended writes.
- Async reclamation CPU/GPU cycles: reclamation consumes spare CPU/GPU bandwidth and can increase overall resource usage. We mitigate by rate-limiting and running reclamation during known low-CPU windows or when autoscaler detects spare capacity.
- Compaction vs eviction speed: background compaction reduces fragmentation and future evictions but can delay immediate availability of memory. We bound compaction window and fall back to simple slab-eviction when latency SLOs are under threat.

Metrics to track: eviction stalls (ms), percent of batches encountering mid-batch eviction, OOM count per hour, average resident_set_ratio, fragmentation_score, lease-contention-rate, write-path p50/p95 latency, throughput (tokens/s) under long-context workloads.

Why unique vs prior approaches: existing experiments we ran explored page-striping and pipe-lined prefetch. This approach focuses on eliminating on-path destructive operations via leases and moving expensive state mutations offline via epoched reclamation, which preserves continuous-batching latency while improving memory efficiency over time.
technical_notes: Lease token layout: 32-bit monotonic sequence + 16-bit owner id + flags (dirty/pinned)
Lease fast-path: atomic compare-exchange on a 64-bit lease word in GPU-shared metadata; fallback to COW path allocates a new block in the per-GPU allocator
Epoch reclamation: per-GPU epoch counter advanced by scheduler at batch boundaries; reclaimers only retire fragments older than current_epoch - 2 to guarantee in-flight readers are safe
Compaction strategy: minibatch-sized compaction (64KB coalesce windows) so GPU memcpy is amortized across many fragments; full compaction is rare and rate-limited
Prefetch profiles derived from telemetry: short=next 2 micro-batches, medium=next 8 micro-batches, long=30s sliding window for chat-style sessions
acceptance_criteria: No KV corruption regressions in 72h fuzzing + stress harness compared to baseline
<5% increase in steady-state write p95 latency in microbench for uncontended workloads
>15% reduction in mid-batch eviction incidents measured on long-context internal benchmark (context=128k tokens, mixed tenants)
End-to-end p99 latency for streaming requests does not regress more than 10% under simulated production load
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind runtime flag runtime.kv.writer_lease (default off)
Canary rollout: enable on 5% of traffic on dedicated cluster A for 48h; collect metrics and flamegraphs
Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% across 1 week with health gates (OOMs, eviction stalls)
Fallback: automatic disable and fallback to previous code path if p99 latency or OOM spikes beyond threshold
test_plan: Unit tests for lease acquisition/release, lease-expiry edge cases
Integration test: synthetic multi-writer workload that previously reproduced corruption; verify correctness with writer_lease enabled
Load test: 72-hour soak on dedicated cluster with mixed tenants and long-context suite
Fault injection: force reclaim-workers to be delayed and ensure scheduler back-pressure prevents OOM
